ABSTRACT
Overparameterization is central to the success of deep learning, yet the mechanisms by which it
improves optimization remain incompletely understood. We analyze weight-space symmetries in
neural networks and show that overparameterization introduces additional symmetries that benefit
optimization in two distinct ways. First, we prove that these symmetries act as a form of diagonal
preconditioning on the Hessian, enabling the existence of better-conditioned minima within each
equivalence class of functionally identical solutions. Second, we show that overparameterization
increases the probability mass of global minima near typical initializations, making these favorable
solutions more reachable. Experiments support our theoretical predictions: as width increases, the
Hessian trace decreases, condition numbers improve, and convergence accelerates. Our analysis
provides a unified framework for understanding overparameterization and width growth as a geometric
transformation of the loss landscape.

Introduction
Overparameterized neural networks consistently outperform their smaller counterparts in optimization speed and final
performance, even when the target function could be represented by much smaller architectures [Arora et al., 2018, Yang
et al., 2022]. A major line of theory explains this via large-width limits and linearization: sufficiently overparameterized
networks exhibit kernel-like dynamics and provable convergence of first-order methods [Jacot et al., 2018, Allen-Zhu
et al., 2019, Du et al., 2019, Zou et al., 2019, Chizat et al., 2019]. Empirical studies of curvature complement this
picture, showing that overparameterized networks have highly structured Hessian spectra with large near-zero subspaces
and few data-dependent outliers [Sagun et al., 2017, Ghorbani et al., 2019].
The loss landscape is also shaped by symmetry: neural networks possess large groups of function-preserving reparame-
terizations (permutations, rescalings, and more structured invariances) that induce equivalence classes of weights and
manifolds of functionally identical minima [Simsek et al., 2021, Kunin et al., 2021, Grigsby et al., 2023, Brea et al.,
2019]. These symmetries complicate naive geometric notions such as “sharpness” [Dinh et al., 2017] and help explain
why seemingly distinct solutions can be connected by low-loss paths [Garipov et al., 2018, Draxler et al., 2018].
This paper sits at the intersection of these two perspectives. We provide a more comprehensive characterization of the
weight-space symmetries due to overparameterization, building on Simsek et al. [2021], and show they aid optimization
through two mechanisms:
Mechanism 1: Diagonal Preconditioning. The eigenvalues of the Hessian H after a symmetry transformation are the
same as those for K1/2HK1/2, where K is a diagonal matrix that depends on the symmetry transformations. The right
choice of K can improve the Hessian conditioning, especially if eigenvectors are approximately axis-aligned.
Mechanism 2: Volume Growth. Overparameterization increases the total volume of global minima near typical
initializations; specifically, the probability of initializing within ϵ of a minimum grows with width once the network
is sufficiently wide. Adding parameters introduces new symmetries that expand the equivalence class, making well-
conditioned, reachable minima more abundant.

• We characterize overparameterization symmetries for deep linear networks and general activations using
a matrix groupoid, building on Simsek et al. [2021]. For ReLU networks, we identify a new family of

Teacher–Student Networks.
To cleanly separate optimization from representation and generalization, we use a

Importantly, our theoretical results are not limited to this teacher-student setting. The universal approximation theorems
imply that any function can be represented by some neural network of minimal width. Teacher-student networks make
this realizability explicit.

Characterizing Overparameterization Symmetries
We begin by noting the definition of overparameterization used in this work, following Simsek et al. [2021]. We say a
neural network is overparameterized if it has greater width than required to represent a given function. This is a natural
notion representing having excess capacity when studying optimization to a given function rather than over a dataset. It
is related but distinct from the notion broadly relating the number of parameters to data samples.

The Overparameterization Groupoid
The symmetry transformations form a groupoid rather than a group. A groupoid is a set of composable transformations
following the group axioms that need not be defined on all objects. There are two reasons for using a groupoid: (1)
Partial composition: A transformation τa→b : Θa →Θb can only compose with transformations originating from
width b. (2) Restricted inverses: We cannot contract beyond the minimal width needed to represent the function. If
a network already represents the function at minimal width nf, there is no inverse operation that reduces the width
further.
We remark that even some weight-space symmetries at a fixed width can be viewed as “local” or groupoid symmetries;
Grigsby et al. [2023] provide a detailed analysis of such hidden symmetries in ReLU networks.
Let OL
nf denote the groupoid of overparameterization operations on networks with L hidden layers and minimum
functional width nf. The key property is that the function is preserved across the orbit: fθ = fθ′ for any θ′ ∈θ · OL

9
Experiments
We support our theoretical predictions with three families of experiments: small-network theory validation where global
minima are guaranteed, student-teacher experiments across MLP, CNN, and Transformer architectures, and direct data
fitting without a teacher. In all cases we train student networks of increasing width and compute Hessian properties
at convergence. Unless stated otherwise, we use µP for width-consistent learning rate scaling Yang et al. [2022] and
report results averaged over 3 seeds. Full details are in Appendix L.
9.1
Theory Validation
We directly test Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 5.3 by training small networks to zero loss with L-BFGS, guaranteeing
convergence to a global minimum. To rule out global minima outside the symmetry orbit of the teacher, we use an
activation from Simsek et al. [2021] for which all global minima of the teacher–student loss are related by the splitting
symmetries we study. Figure 6 shows the Hessian predicted by Theorem 6.1 matches the empirically measured Hessian
to within 0.03% in Tr(H), pdet(H), and ω. Figure 3 confirms the eigenvalue interlacing of Theorem 5.3: teacher
and student eigenvalues alternate, with two additional near-zero eigenvalues from splitting. Post-optimization weights
exhibit the predicted structure (Figure 7; see also Figure 11 in Appendix L): neurons cluster around teacher win values,
with outgoing weights summing to the teacher’s value and 0-type neurons filling the remainder.
9.2
Student-Teacher Experiments
These experiments test whether the Hessian improvements predicted by our theory persist at practical scale and across
architectures. Figure 5 shows MLP students trained with SGD and Adam: condition number, top eigenvalue, AM/GM
ratio, and steps to convergence all improve monotonically with width. The same trends hold across depths (Appendix L).
CNN and Transformer results (Figure 13, Appendix L) show the same monotone improvement; our theory applies
directly to the MLP subspace of Transformer weights, which comprises the majority of parameters.
9.3
Direct Data Fitting
To test whether the improvements depend on the teacher-student setup, we train networks directly on data. Figure 8
shows MLPs on California Housing regression and ConvNets on CIFAR-10 classification; the model cannot fully overfit
in the latter setting. Conditioning improves with width in both cases, extending the result to settings without a teacher
and to mildly underparameterized regimes.
10
Discussion
10.1
Implications for Optimization
Our analysis is an existence result: we characterize which minima exist and their geometric properties, rather than
proving which minima gradient descent converges to. This distinction is deliberate. Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 6.1
establish that overparameterization guarantees the existence of minima with improved conditioning and sufficient
volume, while Section 8 shows these minima occupy increasing probability mass near initialization. Poorly-conditioned
minima with small volume may also exist, but they are both harder to reach and harder to converge to, so optimization
algorithms tend to naturally bypass them. Stochastic gradient noise provides additional selection pressure, destabilizing
convergence in sharp, poorly-conditioned basins.
This is corroborated by Figure 16, where the negligible gap between the mean and best student conditioning suggests that
the mere existence of well-conditioned minima is sufficient to improve practical convergence. In practical optimization,
early stopping within a well-conditioned basin suffices, and overparameterization makes such basins more abundant. A
possible connection to plasticity loss in continual learning is discussed in Appendix I.
10.2
Implications for Generalization
Our framework may also shed light on generalization. Consider noisy training data {xi, yi} generated by some simple
ground truth function f with noise: yi = f(xi) + ζ. The width required to overfit on {xi, yi} is typically much larger
than the width needed to represent f. As a result, the global minima corresponding to f have larger symmetry orbits
and greater volume than those corresponding to overfitting solutions. This provides a counting argument for why
overparameterized networks generalize: they converge to simpler functions not because they have lower loss, but
because their minima are more numerous and easier to optimize.

Wideness of Minima and Anthropic Principle in Optimization
There is an old idea in machine learning that generalizing minima are wide [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997].
However, considering parameter space symmetries it is clear this picture is incomplete: using symmetry transformations
we can construct narrow minima that generalize Dinh et al. [2017]. A more plausible explanation supported by our
findings is that the implication is in the other direction: wide minima represent simpler functions and simpler functions
generalize. This suggests the wonderful coincidence of deep learning is these generalizing minima also happen to be
favored by our optimization process.
11
Conclusion
We show that overparameterization benefits optimization through two distinct mechanisms: diagonal preconditioning of
the Hessian and increased volume of minima near initialization. Our theoretical results are data and optimizer agnostic,
depending only on the symmetry structure of the architecture which prescribes the geometry of the loss landscape.
Impact Statement
This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal
consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Notes on Plasticity Loss
A direct application of our framework concerns plasticity loss in continual learning. When optimization converges to a
simple function, the solution sits on the low-width diagonal of the overparameterization groupoid (Figure 2), and the
locally flat directions of the Hessian coincide with the tangent space of its symmetry orbit. The orbit is invariant under
gradient descent because the gradient is equivariant under the stabilizer, and weight decay or gradient noise tightens the
resulting constraint. Once the objective changes, the optimizer remains confined to the orbit and cannot recruit the
dormant width needed to fit the new task.
Ziyin [2023] previously analyzed this trapping mechanism for permutation, rescaling, and rotation symmetries under
weight decay or noise, and explicitly linked it to plasticity loss. A more detailed and concurrent dynamical systems
treatment appears in Joudaki et al. [2025].

Related Work
Geometry of overparameterization. Sussmann [1992] showed early on that for minimal-width networks, weights
are determined up to permutation and sign-flip symmetries, so these discrete symmetries are the only source of non-
uniqueness when the network is not overparameterized. Simsek et al. [2021] extended this to the overparameterized
setting, identifying the continuous symmetries (neuron splitting and merging) that arise when width exceeds the
functional minimum; their work provides the foundation for our analysis. Kunin et al. [2021] take a complementary
view through conservation laws: each continuous symmetry of the loss induces a conserved quantity along gradient flow,
analogous to Noether’s theorem, which constrains training dynamics beyond the static geometry of minima. Grigsby
et al. [2023] catalog additional “hidden” symmetries in ReLU networks that arise from the piecewise-linear activation
structure, including symmetries that exist only at specific weight configurations (e.g., when a neuron’s pre-activation is
zero on all training data).
Loss landscape structure. Cooper [2021] proves that for networks with d parameters and n data points (d > n),
the global minima generically form a (d −n)-dimensional submanifold rather than isolated points. Nguyen [2019]
shows that all sublevel sets of the loss are connected under mild overparameterization, ruling out “bad local valleys.”
Empirically, Garipov et al. [2018] and Draxler et al. [2018] independently found that minima from different training
runs can be connected by paths of near-constant loss. Entezari et al. [2022] conjectured that after accounting for
permutation symmetry, SGD solutions from different initializations lie in a single basin; Ainsworth et al. [2023] gave
practical algorithms for aligning models modulo these symmetries. Our work adds to this picture by showing that
overparameterization symmetries not only connect minima but reshape the curvature at those minima.
Convergence theory. Jacot et al. [2018] introduced the neural tangent kernel (NTK), showing that in the infinite-width
limit, training reduces to kernel regression with a fixed kernel. Building on this, several works proved that gradient
descent on sufficiently wide networks converges to global minima at a linear rate: Du et al. [2019] for deep residual
networks, Allen-Zhu et al. [2019] for general deep networks, and Zou et al. [2019] for SGD on deep ReLU networks.
These results typically require the width to be polynomial in the number of samples and the depth. Chizat et al. [2019]
showed that this favorable convergence arises from a “lazy training” regime where parameters stay near initialization
and the model behaves as its linearization, which can underperform feature learning in practice. Our approach is
different: rather than analyzing dynamics in a linearized regime, we characterize the geometric properties (conditioning,
volume) of minima at finite width.
Implicit acceleration and deep linear networks. Deep linear networks, where f(x) = WL · · · W1x, are a standard
testbed for optimization theory. Saxe et al. [2014] derived exact learning dynamics, showing that depth creates
saddle-to-saddle transitions that progressively learn singular value components. Arora et al. [2018] showed that the
resulting dynamics acts as implicit acceleration: the factored parameterization preconditions the optimization of the
end-to-end matrix, with the effect depending on the singular values of the current solution. Ghosh et al. [2025] extend
this analysis beyond the edge of stability, characterizing oscillatory dynamics at large learning rates. We extend the
preconditioning perspective in a different direction, from depth to width and from linear to general activations, showing
that overparameterization symmetries provide diagonal preconditioning on the Hessian.
Conditioning and curvature. Sagun et al. [2017] showed empirically that overparameterized networks have Hessian
spectra with a large bulk of near-zero eigenvalues and a few data-dependent outliers; the near-zero eigenvalues
correspond to flat directions from overparameterization, while the outliers capture the curvature relevant to learning.
Ghorbani et al. [2019] gave a more detailed eigenvalue density analysis, connecting spectral structure to properties
of the data and architecture. Guille-Escuret et al. [2023] found that optimization paths in neural networks have
surprisingly simple geometry despite the non-convexity of the loss. Yang et al. [2022] showed through µP that wider
networks are more robust to learning rate choices, suggesting that width improves conditioning in a way that reduces
hyperparameter sensitivity. Classical results on diagonal preconditioning [Forsythe and Straus, 1955, Collobert, 2004]
show that coordinate rescaling can improve the condition number when eigenvectors are not uniformly distributed
across coordinates; this underpins our analysis in Section 5.3.
Normalization and symmetry exploitation. Several practical methods explicitly navigate weight-space symmetries
to find better-conditioned parameterizations. Weight normalization [Salimans and Kingma, 2016] decouples weight
magnitude from direction, moving along the rescaling orbit. Path-SGD [Neyshabur et al., 2015] uses a path-regularized
objective invariant to rescaling, so the trajectory is not distorted by the parameterization choice within an equivalence
class. Mishkin et al. [2025] introduced level-set teleportation, which solves for a better-conditioned point on the same
level set by optimizing over the symmetry group. All of these can be viewed as searching within a symmetry orbit for
favorable parameterizations.

Hessian Computation
After convergence, we compute the Hessian eigenspectrum using the Lanczos algorithm with full reorthogonalization,
which efficiently approximates the eigenvalue distribution via Hessian-vector products without forming the full matrix.
For small networks used in theory validation we additionally compute the full Hessian exactly via finite differences to
verify the Lanczos estimates. We extract: the complete eigenvalue spectrum, trace, top eigenvalue, condition number
(λmax/λ+
min), pseudo-determinant (product of nonzero eigenvalues), and the AM/GM ratio of positive eigenvalues.
Gradient norms are also recorded at the final iterate.

Abstract: Overparameterization is central to the success of deep learning, yet the mechanisms by which it improves optimization remain incompletely understood. We analyze weight-space symmetries in neural networks and show that overparameterization introduces additional symmetries that benefit optimization in two distinct ways. First, we prove that these symmetries act as a form of diagonal preconditioning on the Hessian, enabling the existence of better-conditioned minima within each equivalence class of functionally identical solutions. Second, we show that overparameterization increases the probability mass of global minima near typical initializations, making these favorable solutions more reachable. Experiments support our theoretical predictions: as width increases, the Hessian trace decreases, condition numbers improve, and convergence accelerates. Our analysis provides a unified framework for understanding overparameterization and width growth as a geometric transformation of the loss landscape.
